name: gnu-smalltalk
why: A GNU Smalltalk environment opens a door into a live object-oriented language with a long, influential history.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Smalltalk is a free implementation of the Smalltalk-80 language, with a command-line virtual machine called gst. You give it Smalltalk source as files on the command line or on standard input, and it compiles and runs that code. Output is printed to the terminal, and results of top-level expressions are echoed at the st> prompt unless you use -q. The homepage describes it as running on most Unix systems and anywhere a POSIX-compliance library is available. The manual says the goal is a complete system for writing scripts in Smalltalk, and it also has a GTK-based GUI environment (GTK and VisualGST).
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says an uncommon feature is that it is well-versed to scripting tasks and headless processing. The manual says it emphasizes rapid prototyping over the graphical environment of other Smalltalks, and aims to be a language for scripts that is clear, aesthetically pleasing, and philosophically appealing, in place of tasks usually given to scripting languages.
brief.how_it_works: gst runs a virtual machine on a binary image file (gst.im). On startup it checks that the image is up to date against the kernel source files, and rebuilds it from those files if it is stale. Files given on the command line run in order and then it exits. The manual also describes a larger startup sequence: site-pre.st, ~/.st/pre.st, the snapshot, then ~/.st/init.st. The class reference in the library docs is generated by a Smalltalk program from the library source.

commands_seen.context: Invocation synopsis from the user's guide. Files are run in order and gst exits at end of file. With no file, gst reads standard input.
Runs a file as a script with arguments, described as equivalent to gst -q file -a args...
Shebang line for a Smalltalk script file that runs directly. The manual also shows a #! /bin/sh variant that uses an exec "gst" line.
Runs the regression test suite from the top-level source directory. Any output other than the names of the test files indicates a problem.
Typed at the st> prompt to exit. Ctrl-d also exits when reading from standard input.
Example input from the syntax section. It prints the decimal value of octal 300 and hex FFFF, each followed by a newline.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula installs three executables: gst, gst-blox, and gst-config. I saw documentation only for gst; I did not find docs for gst-blox or gst-config. No accounts, hardware, or extra runtimes are mentioned. On first run gst builds gst.im from the kernel files, and it can load ~/.st/kernel overrides, ~/.st/pre.st and ~/.st/init.st. The SMALLTALK_IMAGE and SMALLTALK_KERNEL environment variables and the --no-user-files flag also change this. Images only load on systems with the same pointer size, so an x86-64 image will not load on 32-bit x86.
brief.standout: Most Smalltalks are built around an interactive graphical image. This one treats the image as a snapshot you can rebuild from source, and it aims at scripting and headless use. The manual also says the class reference is generated from the library source by a Smalltalk program. The language follows the Blue Book closely, with a few extensions such as generators built on continuations, namespaces, and a built-in Perl-style regex engine.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages do not show a release date or last commit. The homepage footer reads 'Updated: $Date: 2019/11/11' and the copyright line says 2007, but those dates belong to the web page, not to project activity. The homepage links to a Savannah project page and FTP release sites, which I did not fetch.
brief.caveats: The VM is GPL, so programs that bundle it must also be GPL. The system class libraries are LGPL, and the manual gives a specific reading of how LGPL applies to images. The manual says the startup sequence is complicated. Ctrl-c during startup aborts it. The regex engine is 8-bit clean and does not fully support Unicode even when the I18N package is loaded. The GUI is GTK-based and the manual describes it only briefly. Several package entries in the manual's package list are empty.
quotes: GNU Smalltalk is a free implementation of the Smalltalk-80 language which runs on most versions on Unix and, in general, everywhere you can find a POSIX-compliance library.
An uncommon feature of it is that it is well-versed to scripting tasks and headless processing.
Unlike other Smalltalks (including Smalltalk-80), GNU Smalltalk emphasizes Smalltalk's rapid prototyping features rather than the graphical and easy-to-use nature of the programming environment
